name: Brithenig
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.verdict: a reachable source states the stress pattern
earlier_scan.source_named: Wikipedia, 'Brithenig' (read 2026-08-31; summarizing Andrew Smith's The Page of Brithenig)

new_statements.quote: Stress in Brithenig is placed on the ultimate, or last syllable, for example, afwr, love, is pronounced as 'a-FWR' [a'vur], not 'A-fur' ['avur]. In diphthongs, the first vowel is pronounced as a stressed or unstressed vowel depending on whether it occured in the stressed syllable or not. [...] Brithenig sometimes accents words with a circumflex, called a teithith, or little roof. Although the accent is always pronounced as 'long', more often than not it appears to be purely grammatical, for example, lla and llâ.
new_statements.citation: Smith, Andrew. 'Alphabet and combined letters', The Page of Brithenig (creator's grammar website; mirror at steen.free.fr/brithenig, hosted by Jan van Steenbergen since 2010, server Last-Modified 2015-11-19; original hobbit.griffler.co.nz archived 2009-05-28). Cited in the literature as Smith (2007a).

new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence:
Opened (raw HTML lines 141-149). Verbatim there: "Stress in Brithenig is placed on the ultimate, or last syllable, for example, afwr, love, is pronounced as 'a-FWR' [a'vur], not 'A-fur' ['avur]. In diphthongs, the first vowel is pronounced as a stressed or unstressed vowel depending on whether it occured in the stressed syllable or not" (source has NO full stop after "or not" before the next

; the report's quote adds one and bridges with "[..]" - the only differences). Next paragraph verbatim: "Brithenig sometimes accents words with a circumflex, called a teithith, or little roof. Although the accent is always pronounced as 'long', more often than not it appears…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the last syllable of the word (the creator's deliberate contrast with Welsh penultimate stress; e.g. afwr 'love' [a'vur], yscol 'school' stressed on -col). Stressed a, e, i, w have full values; unstressed a and e reduce to schwa, unstressed i to [ɪ]. The circumflex marks vowel length or a grammatical distinction, not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-initial y 'is often unstressed and when preceded by a word ending in a vowel it often elides' (consistent with final stress, since initial y- is a non-final syllable). Monosyllables ending in -Cr/-Cl get an echo vowel (llifr 'book' = ['ɬivr] / 'llifir'), which the source transcribes with stress on the first (only) syllable; no lexical exceptions to final stress are listed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated for isolated words; the page also notes phrase-level elisions (sa es > sa's) but says nothing about phrasal accent. Constructed language: the statement is the designer's stipulation, not an observation of speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Brithenig is a constructed (artistic/alternate-history) language created by Andrew Smith in 1996; Glottolog files it under family 'Artificial Language' (brit1244, ISO bzt, country NZ). The statement is the creator's own design rule, not a description of a speech community, so the catalog's policy on conlangs decides whether it belongs; the rule itself is unambiguous and first-hand. No dialect issue (the page mentions a 'standard dialect' only for ae/oe vowel realisation).

sources.note: Final paragraph: 'Stress in Brithenig is placed on the ultimate, or last syllable, for example, afwr, love, is pronounced as a-FWR [a'vur], not A-fur ['avur].' Diphthong first-vowel quality follows the stressed/unstressed status of its syllable; word-initial y 'is often unstressed' and elides after a vowel; the circumflex (teithith) marks length/grammar, not stress; unstressed a, e reduce to [ə].
